title: The applause that disrupted nothing — yet still led to an arrest
excerpt: The city commission of Emporia, Kansas, has endured countless hours of public criticism.
content_html:
The city commission of Emporia, Kansas, has endured countless hours of public criticism. What it could not endure was a few seconds of clapping.

At its July 22 meeting, citizens contested a proposed data center, briefly applauding between public comments as one speaker left the microphone and another approached. Commissioners sometimes ignored the applause and other times warned the audience to stop. But their warnings soon expanded to cover even more muted reactions like finger-snapping and a woman in the back of the room silently waving her hands.

When high school physics teacher Lux Claridge clapped five times for a speaker, a commissioner told officers to remove the next person who clapped. But instead of waiting for another round of applause, officers immediately ordered Claridge to leave. After refusing, Claridge was physically removed, arrested, and booked on charges of disorderly conduct and interference with law enforcement.

In other words, a citizen was thrown to the ground, arrested, and removed from a public meeting for endorsing criticism of local government in a non-disruptive manner.

Emporia’s written public-comment rules don’t ban applause. They authorize removal when someone “fails to comply with public comment procedure, speaks out of turn, or is otherwise disruptive,” and continues after a warning. To be sure, government bodies can adopt clear, viewpoint-neutral rules against conduct that actually disrupts a meeting — preventing speakers from being heard, hijacking the floor when not recognized to speak, or otherwise preventing the government from conducting its business.

But that’s not what happened in the Emporia Municipal Courtroom. None of the clapping, including Claridge’s, materially disrupted the meeting. Each burst of applause lasted only a few seconds during the interval between public comments. No speaker was interrupted or delayed. The meeting continued moving forward. The only disruption came from the arrest of Claridge and the meeting recess that followed.

The incident illustrates a recurring problem with vague decorum policies for public meetings. They give officials room to recast expression they dislike as “disruption,” and tend to be enforced most aggressively when criticism stings. It’s hard to believe the commission would have reacted the same way to brief applause for comments praising city officials. But even if so, the fact remains that none of the clapping was “otherwise disruptive.” And Claridge’s refusal to leave cannot retroactively supply the missing disruption to justify removal in the first place.

Officials can require order — the First Amendment does not force them to let meetings become ungovernable — but they can’t demand monastic silence and perfect stillness from everyone in the room.

Emporia’s own policy says public comment is intended to “provide citizens with an opportunity to provide input to the governing body on matters of city business.” Brief, nondisruptive audience reactions do exactly that. A few seconds of applause signal support for a speaker and the intensity of public sentiment. Applause can also give residents who don’t make a formal comment themselves a way to convey their opinions.

Local government meetings are where people confront decisions about their neighborhoods, schools, taxes, utilities, and homes. Officials can require order — the First Amendment does not force them to let meetings become ungovernable — but they can’t demand monastic silence and perfect stillness from everyone in the room, then treat any audible or visible reaction as disorder.

If no speaker is drowned out, no one loses their speaking time, and the meeting keeps moving, where is the disruption? When brief applause becomes grounds for removal and arrest, it’s worth asking whether officials are preserving order, or simply punishing dissent.

content_html_zh:
堪萨斯州恩波里亚市委员会承受了无数个小时的公众批评。 它无法忍受的是几秒钟的鼓掌。

在 7 月 22 日的会议上，公民对拟建的数据中心提出了质疑，当一位发言者离开麦克风、另一位发言者走近时，公众发表评论时短暂鼓掌。 委员们有时会忽视掌声，有时会警告观众停止。 但他们的警告很快扩大到包括更多无声的反应，比如打响指和房间后面的一个女人默默地挥手。

当高中物理老师勒克斯·克拉里奇（Lux Claridge）为演讲者鼓掌五次时，一名专员告诉警察将下一个鼓掌的人赶走。 但警察没有等待另一场掌声，而是立即命令克拉里奇离开。 在拒绝后，克拉里奇被驱逐、逮捕，并以行为不检和干扰执法罪名被立案登记。

换句话说，一名公民因以不间断的方式支持对地方政府的批评而被摔倒在地、被捕并被赶出公开集会。

恩波里亚的书面公众评论规则并不禁止鼓掌。 当有人“不遵守公众意见程序、说话不按顺序或有其他破坏性行为”时，他们会授权将其删除，并在发出警告后继续删除。 可以肯定的是，政府机构可以针对实际上扰乱会议的行为采取明确的、观点中立的规则——阻止发言者被听到，在不被认可发言时劫持发言权，或者以其他方式阻止政府开展业务。

但这并不是恩波里亚市法庭发生的事情。 包括克拉里奇在内的所有掌声都没有对会议产生实质性干扰。 在公众发表评论的间隙，每次爆发的掌声只持续了几秒钟。 没有发言者被打断或延迟。 会议继续向前推进。 唯一的干扰来自克拉里奇的被捕以及随后的会议休会。

该事件说明了公共会议礼仪政策模糊不清的反复出现的问题。 它们为官员们提供了将他们不喜欢的言论重新定义为“破坏”的空间，并且在批评刺痛时往往会得到最严厉的执行。 很难相信该委员会会对赞扬市政府官员的评论做出同样的反应，短暂鼓掌。 但即便如此，事实仍然是，没有任何鼓掌是“否则具有破坏性的”。 克拉里奇拒绝离开并不能追溯​​性地提供缺失的干扰，以证明其首先离开的合理性。

官员们可以要求秩序——第一修正案并没有强迫他们让会议变得失控——但他们不能要求房间里的每个人都保持修道院般的沉默和完全的静止。

恩波里亚自己的政策称，公众意见的目的是“为公民提供就城市商业事务向管理机构提供意见的机会”。 简短、无干扰的观众反应正是这样做的。 几秒钟的掌声表明了对演讲者的支持以及公众情绪的强烈程度。 掌声还可以为那些自己没有发表正式评论的居民提供表达意见的方式。

地方政府会议是人们就社区、学校、税收、公用事业和住房做出决定的地方。 官员们可以要求秩序——第一修正案并没有强迫他们让会议变得失控——但他们不能要求房间里的每个人保持修道院般的沉默和完全的静止，然后将任何听到或看到的反应视为混乱。

如果没有发言者被淹没，没有人失去发言时间，并且会议继续进行，那么中断在哪里？ 当短暂的掌声成为驱逐和逮捕的理由时，值得一问的是，官员们是在维护秩序，还是只是在惩罚异见人士。
